nameStory: The Carolina Saddlebags gets its memorable name from the distinctive dark patches at the base of its hindwings that look exactly like old-fashioned saddlebags draped over a horse's back. The 'Carolina' part refers to where this species was first scientifically described, though these dragonflies actually range throughout much of eastern North America.
description: Carolina Saddlebags are large, impressive dragonflies that patrol open areas with strong, steady flight. They have amber-tinted wings with distinctive dark brown or black patches at the base of their hindwings that really do resemble saddlebags. Their bodies are typically reddish-brown to amber colored, and they can reach about 2.5 to 3 inches in length with a wingspan of around 4 inches. These are among our more noticeable dragonflies, often seen gliding and hovering over ponds, lakes, and wetlands.

idTips.label: Saddlebag wing patches
idTips.description: Look for the dark brown to black patches at the base of the hindwings that look like pouches hanging down - these are unmistakable and much more prominent than similar markings on other dragonflies

idTips.label: Amber wing tint
idTips.description: The wings have a noticeable amber or golden tint, especially visible when backlit by sunlight, giving them a warm, honey-colored glow

idTips.label: Reddish-brown body
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen are warm reddish-brown to amber colored, sometimes appearing almost rusty in bright light

idTips.label: Strong gliding flight
idTips.description: Flies with confident, steady wingbeats and long glides, often patrolling back and forth over water with less erratic movement than smaller dragonflies

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: One of our bigger dragonflies - about the length of your index finger with wings that span nearly the width of your palm

habitat: Carolina Saddlebags prefer large, open bodies of water including ponds, lakes, slow-moving rivers, and marshes throughout New England's lowlands and coastal areas. You'll often spot them patrolling over the water's surface or perched on emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They favor areas with plenty of open airspace for hunting and minimal tree cover directly over the water.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May and early June. Look for them during warm, sunny afternoons when they're most active over their breeding waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from July through August. This is the best time to observe their distinctive flight patterns and saddlebag wing markings as they patrol territories and mate.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through September and sometimes into early October during warm spells. Late summer individuals often appear more worn with tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: No adults present. Nymphs overwinter underwater in pond and lake sediments, developing for the following year's emergence.

funFact: Carolina Saddlebags are incredible long-distance migrants that can travel hundreds of miles, sometimes appearing in huge swarms during migration that can actually show up on weather radar - just like flocks of birds!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Black Saddlebags, but Carolina Saddlebags have amber-tinted wings and reddish-brown bodies, while Black Saddlebags have clearer wings and darker, more blackish bodies. Memory trick: 'Carolina = Caramel colored' for the warm amber tones.
compareHints: Among the saddlebag dragonflies in New England, Carolina Saddlebags are distinguished by their warm amber wing tint and reddish-brown body coloration. Black Saddlebags are larger with clearer wings and much darker bodies, while the rare Striped Saddlebags have distinctive yellow stripes on their thorax. The wing saddlebags on Carolina Saddlebags are also typically more brownish than the jet-black patches seen on Black Saddlebags.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black Saddlebags have much more extensive and darker wing patches than their relatives - Carolina Saddlebags show brown or amber coloring in their wing patches rather than solid black, while Striped Saddlebags have distinctive striping patterns.
